clue.text: Grant I'd applied for in business

indicators.note: applied in the sense of put to work or bent into use, telling us to rework these letters

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone applies for a grant to help their company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'applied' shuffles GRANT and ID into the answer; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm that is still buying and selling goods is operating as a going concern.

parts.note: the idiom for something superior, read literally as a joint of beef taken from the upper part of the leg

explanation.surface: Praise for something superior to everything else.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase usually means excellent; here it is a butcher's cut taken from the top of the leg.
explanation.definitionFit: Topside is the beef joint cut from the upper inner thigh, literally above other cuts.

clue.text: Took on commercial work and spread out

parts.note: a commercial is an advertisement, an ad
op is short for opus, a musical work
to ted is to spread out mown hay for drying

explanation.surface: Someone accepted advertising work and broadened their business.
explanation.walkthrough: TED, an old farming verb for scattering hay to dry, is the piece most solvers will not know.
explanation.definitionFit: To adopt a child, an idea or a policy is to take it on as your own.

indicators.note: the name is trapped inside the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: A girl is hit in a pointless exchange of fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught in' picks the run spanning crossfiRE NEedlessly.
explanation.definitionFit: Irene is a female first name, so a girl is a fair example.

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go around the single letter
madly says the letters of the next word go wild and rearrange

explanation.surface: A boatman slobbering wildly, apparently an Englishman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Madly' turns DROOLING into GONDOLIR, and 'about' puts it round E.
explanation.definitionFit: The man who rows a Venetian canal boat with a single oar is a type of boatman.

clue.text: Common plant types, fifty in number

parts.note: genera are classes of plants in biological classification
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A botanist notes some fifty everyday plant groups.
explanation.walkthrough: GENERA is the plural of genus, a ranking above species.
explanation.definitionFit: Something general is widespread, shared by most, so ordinary and common.

definitions.meaning: a command telling someone to rise to their feet
clothing or an outfit, often an odd one

explanation.surface: A regular bank instruction to buy equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing order' looks like a regular bank payment; read it as an order to stand.
explanation.definitionFit: The command to rise is 'get up!', and an outfit is a getup.

parts.note: suggests the aurora, but means the star that sits above the pole and guides travellers

explanation.surface: A question about the glow seen in polar skies.
explanation.walkthrough: Polar light suggests the aurora borealis; it is Polaris, the star nearly above the North Pole.
explanation.definitionFit: Polaris, the bright pole star, is a celestial light at the north celestial pole.

definitions.meaning: a set sequence of actions, such as a performer's act or daily schedule
done by habit, in the ordinary customary way

explanation.surface: A broadcast made in the normal way.
explanation.definitionFit: A routine is a fixed sequence of actions; as an adjective it means ordinary or habitual.

indicators.note: the word relates is told to change, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A theatre note: this Shakespearean part relates to transformation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to change' rearranges RELATES.
explanation.definitionFit: Laertes is Ophelia's brother in Hamlet, a character in a Shakespeare play.

parts.note: not an internet stream but a radio show carried by listeners on the telephone line

explanation.surface: A question about streaming a show over the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: On-line suggests the internet, but the line is a telephone line: callers ring in and go on air.
explanation.definitionFit: A show where listeners call the studio is broadcast down telephone lines.

clue.text: Run over Yorkshire banker causing anguish

indicators.note: over means the word for run is turned back to front

parts.note: to trot is to run at a gentle pace
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire, and a river is a banker because it has banks

explanation.surface: A runner goes past a Yorkshire bank clerk, who is upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' reverses TROT to TORT. A 'banker' is a crossword river, here the Ure in Yorkshire, northern England; 'causing' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Torture means extreme suffering, physical or mental, just as anguish is.

clue.text: Prepared to punish European for it

indicators.note: prepared signals that the letters are made ready in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is ready to discipline a European for some offence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prepared' shuffles TOPUNISH with E. 'for it' means about to be punished.
explanation.definitionFit: Being 'for it' and being in deep trouble are both idioms for facing punishment.

clue.text: Jack including one in present show

indicators.note: including means the word for present takes the letter inside it

parts.note: to host a programme is to present a show
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Jack takes part in presenting a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a name; it is the verb, to jack up or raise.
explanation.definitionFit: To jack a car is to lift it, as with a winch or pulley.

indicators.note: somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Money set aside that has partly collapsed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somewhat' picks the run spanning fallEN DOWn.
explanation.definitionFit: To endow an institution is to provide it with a lasting income, to finance it.

clue.text: Went today to order domestic fowl

indicators.note: the letters are put to order, arranged in a new sequence

explanation.surface: Someone went out today to order a chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to order' rearranges WENTTODAY.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wyandotte is an American breed of chicken kept for eggs and meat.

clue.text: I I nip a stem off flowering plant

indicators.note: off in the sense of gone bad or wrong, so these letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener snips the stalk from a plant in bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' shuffles INIPASTEM into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Impatiens is the genus of busy Lizzie and balsam, garden plants with bright blooms.

indicators.note: before puts the attack word ahead of the rest

parts.note: a push is a military attack, an offensive
a bout is a fight, as in boxing

explanation.surface: A bully is aggressive before any scrap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'offensive' is a noun here, a military attack, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To push someone about is to order them around roughly, to intimidate them.

indicators.note: pinching means the shortened bird grips the man's name inside it
almost means the last letter of the bird is dropped

parts.note: a thrush is a songbird
Esau, the son of Isaac, is a crossword's favourite man, as he is described as a hairy man in Genesis

explanation.surface: A bird nearly steals a man's book.
explanation.walkthrough: Esau is the hairy man of Genesis, often a crossword 'man'; the surface's bird and book are unrelated.
explanation.definitionFit: A thesaurus is a reference volume of synonyms.

indicators.note: initial selects only the opening letter of the teacher word

parts.note: an earful is a scolding, a telling-off

explanation.surface: A pupil is upset at being told off by the teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initial' takes T from teacher's; 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A tearful person is weeping or close to it, upset.

clue.text: One feels it as energy flow

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
motion is movement, a flow

explanation.surface: A description of a feeling as a stream of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One feels it' is the whole definition: feelings are what we feel; 'as' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Joy, anger and fear are feelings, experienced inwardly by a person.

clue.text: Fast mover's double-handed serve going in

indicators.note: going in means the serve word is placed inside the doubled letter
double says the hand letter appears twice, side by side

parts.note: R stands for right, as in the right hand
an ace is an unreturnable tennis serve

explanation.surface: A tennis player's two-handed serve lands in for a winner.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is tennis: a two-handed shot and a serve that is in. The 's of mover's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A racer is a horse, car or runner built for speed.

indicators.note: bypassing means the move word passes by and ends up after the article

parts.note: chic means stylish, smart
a go is a turn or move in a game

explanation.surface: A clever play that passes over something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart move' reads as one phrase meaning a clever step, but it splits into two pieces, and 'bypassing' sends the move past the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicago is a large US city in Illinois.

parts.note: to rag is to tease or mock
a time is a period, an era

explanation.surface: A dated style of music that is mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mock' looks like an adjective; it is the verb, to rag.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragtime is a syncopated piano style of the early twentieth century.

indicators.note: fills means the zero goes into the middle of the hungry word

parts.note: avid means eager, hungry for something
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A hungry duck finds there is nothing to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duck' looks like the bird; it is the verb, to dodge.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck a question or blow is to dodge or evade it.

clue.text: Flier from Britain going on and on

parts.note: B is a standard abbreviation for British, as in BBC
rambling means talking at length without stopping

explanation.surface: A bird from Britain keeps talking endlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The brambling is a finch, a bird, so a flier.

indicators.note: reportedly says the panel word is heard spoken, not seen

parts.note: a board is a panel, as of directors or of wood

explanation.surface: A committee, it is said, is uninterested.
explanation.walkthrough: BOARD and BORED sound alike in standard British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A bored person feels weary and lacks enthusiasm.

definitions.meaning: Sir Arthur ... was Master of the Queen's Music from 1953 to 1975
perfect happiness, as in the ecstasy of paradise

explanation.surface: A former royal composer is now in paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: The Master of the Queen's Music is a British royal post for a composer; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Bliss held the royal post of Master of the Queen's Music; bliss is supreme joy.

clue.text: Flap about trainee mechanic coming round

indicators.note: coming round means the mechanic word encloses the trainee letter

parts.note: a fitter assembles or repairs machinery
L is the learner plate, a sign of someone in training

explanation.surface: A panic as a mechanic in training arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: L comes from the British L-plate shown by learner drivers.
explanation.definitionFit: To flitter is to flutter or move about restlessly.

parts.note: not office forms but art made from folded sheets

explanation.surface: A query about administration.
explanation.walkthrough: Paperwork suggests forms; here it is craft work done with paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of folding sheets into shapes, literally work with paper.

indicators.note: out here means the worn word stays outside, around the bearings

parts.note: a lined face is worn with age
S and E are compass bearings, south and east

explanation.surface: Oil from worn-out bearings in a machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worn out' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'worn' gives the word for wrinkled and 'out' says it sits outside the bearings.
explanation.definitionFit: Linseed oil is pressed from flax seeds and used in paints and varnishes.

clue.text: Trousers made up without right kind of fabric

indicators.note: made up means the letters of the garment word are rearranged
without means one letter is left out of the rearranged word

explanation.surface: Trousers sewn up from something other than the correct cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: TROUSERS less R gives TOUSERS, rearranged by 'made up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tussore is a coarse silk made by wild silkworms.
